questions.question: GitHub Actions vs Jenkins vs GitLab CI — which one and when?
questions.title: GitHub Actions vs Jenkins vs GitLab CI: Hosting, Cost, Lock-in
questions.direct_answer: GitHub Actions wins for repos already on GitHub — zero infra, marketplace ecosystem, generous free tier; weak for self-hosted or compliance-heavy environments. Jenkins wins for self-hosted control, complex pipelines with deep plugin needs, multi-cloud, and air-gapped environments — but you own the maintenance burden. GitLab CI wins as an integrated DevSecOps platform: built-in container registry, security scanning, and Kubernetes integration in one product — best when you want one tool for repo + CI + registry + deploy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical tool selection across team size, infra constraints, and ecosystem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing GitHub Actions for a self-hosted regulated environment without realizing self-hosted runners need similar infra effort to Jenkins
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the runner cost model (per-minute), self-hosted runner security risks, vendor lock-in via composite actions, and the secret-management story per tool

sections.title: Three Tools Solving the Same Problem with Different Priorities
sections.content:
All three run pipelines triggered by repo events: build, test, deploy. The differences are in **where they run**, **what's batteries-included**, and **what you're locked into**.

**GitHub Actions** is YAML pipelines living in `.github/workflows/` of your GitHub repo, running on GitHub-hosted runners (Linux/Windows/macOS) by default. The marketplace ships thousands of reusable actions — Docker login, AWS credential setup, Slack notifications. Pricing: 2,000 free minutes/month for private repos, then per-minute. Self-hosted runners are free but you operate them. Best for teams already on GitHub who want minimum setup and tight integration with PRs, issues, and Codespaces.

**Jenkins** is the original CI server: self-hosted, plugin-based, Groovy or declarative pipelines. Massive plugin ecosystem (1,800+) covers virtually every tool. You run the server, manage agents, patch plugins, handle security. Wins when you need full control — air-gapped environments, compliance requirements forbidding cloud CI, complex multi-org pipelines, or integrations no SaaS tool covers. The cost is operational burden: Jenkins LTS upgrades, plugin compatibility, agent fleet sizing.

**GitLab CI** ships built into GitLab. Pipelines defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. The killer feature is integration: container registry, package registry, security scanning (SAST, DAST, dependency, container), Kubernetes deploy, and observability all in one product. Best when you're consolidating tools and want one source of truth for code, CI, and supply-chain artifacts. Available as SaaS (gitlab.com) or self-hosted (gitlab.com/ce, gitlab.com/ee).

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | GitHub Actions | Jenkins | GitLab CI |
|--------|----------------|---------|-----------|
| **Hosting** | SaaS (GitHub.com) or self-hosted runners | Self-hosted (or CloudBees SaaS) | SaaS (gitlab.com) or self-hosted |
| **Pipeline language** | YAML | Groovy DSL or declarative | YAML |
| **Setup time to first pipeline** | 15 min | 1–3 days (install, configure, plugins) | 30 min |
| **Marketplace / plugins** | 20,000+ actions | 1,800+ plugins | Built-in features (fewer 3rd party) |
| **Pricing model** | Per-minute on GitHub-hosted; free self-hosted | Free OSS, infra cost | Free SaaS tier; self-hosted free |
| **Container registry** | GitHub Container Registry (separate product) | None (use Nexus/Artifactory) | Built-in container + package registry |
| **Security scanning** | Via 3rd-party actions (Snyk, Trivy) | Via plugins | Built-in SAST, DAST, dependency, container |
| **Secrets management** | Repo/org/env secrets, OIDC to cloud | Credentials plugin, Vault integration | CI/CD variables, masked, file-type |
| **Best for** | GitHub-native teams; OSS; tight PR integration | Self-hosted, regulated, complex multi-tool | DevSecOps consolidation; one-tool shop |
| **Lock-in** | High (composite actions tie to GitHub) | Low (Jenkinsfile is portable) | Medium (works only with GitLab) |
| **Vendor risk** | Microsoft/GitHub | Open source, community-driven | GitLab Inc. |

sections.title: Decision Tree: Which to Pick
sections.content:
**Start with the repo platform.** If your code is on GitHub and you're a startup or product team, GitHub Actions is the default — you already have it. Same for GitLab CI if you're on GitLab.

**Pick Jenkins when:**
- **Air-gapped or on-premises with no cloud egress.** Jenkins runs anywhere; SaaS CI tools require cloud connectivity.
- **Heavy compliance requirements** (FedRAMP, government, healthcare without BAA-covered SaaS) where source code cannot leave your perimeter.
- **Multi-cloud, multi-tool ecosystem.** A team running pipelines that touch AWS, GCP, on-prem Kubernetes, mainframe deploys, and proprietary tools — Jenkins's plugin breadth wins.
- **Pre-existing Jenkins investment** with hundreds of pipelines and team expertise; migration cost outweighs benefits.
- **Complex pipeline DSL needs.** Jenkins shared libraries with full Groovy let you encode complex logic that YAML CI/CD makes painful.

**Pick GitLab CI when:**
- **You want one tool for repo + CI + registry + scanning + deploy.** GitLab is the consolidation play.
- **DevSecOps with built-in scanning.** SAST, DAST, dependency, container, and license scanning come included — no plugin assembly required.
- **Regulated environments wanting self-hosted but not Jenkins.** GitLab self-hosted gives you SaaS-like UX with full control.

**Pick GitHub Actions when:**
- **You're on GitHub and want minimum setup.** Default for most teams in 2026.
- **OSS projects.** Free on public repos; the marketplace ecosystem is unmatched.
- **Cloud-native deploy with OIDC.** Actions has first-class OIDC integration with AWS/Azure/GCP — no long-lived secrets needed.
- **Tight integration with PR review.** Actions checks, deployments, and environments integrate deeply with the PR UX.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs Most Teams Miss
sections.content:
**Self-hosted runner security in GitHub Actions.** Self-hosted runners process untrusted PR code. A PR from a fork can run arbitrary code on your runner. Mitigations: never use self-hosted runners on public repos without `pull_request_target` restrictions; use ephemeral runners that destroy themselves after each job; isolate sensitive runners.

**The cost crossover for GitHub Actions.** GitHub-hosted runners are great until you hit ~50,000 minutes/month. Past that, self-hosted runners (on EC2 spot or k8s) become cheaper — but now you own the operational burden, eroding the GitHub Actions advantage.

**Jenkins plugin rot.** A Jenkins instance with 100 plugins is a ticking time bomb. Plugin maintainers go inactive; security advisories pile up; LTS upgrades break combinations. Mature Jenkins teams have a dedicated platform team or migrate to managed (CloudBees CI).

**GitLab CI runner caching.** Jobs are stateless; caching between jobs requires explicit cache configuration that's easy to misconfigure (wrong key, wrong paths). Slow pipelines often trace to cache misses. Use distributed cache (S3, GCS) for shared caching.

**Vendor lock-in via composite actions.** GitHub Actions composite actions and reusable workflows tie your pipeline DNA to GitHub. Migrating off requires rewriting in YAML for another tool. Jenkinsfiles are more portable.

**OIDC adoption.** All three support OIDC federation to cloud providers (no long-lived secrets). GitHub Actions has the cleanest UX; Jenkins requires plugin setup; GitLab supports it but config is verbose. Use OIDC over static credentials wherever possible.

**Concurrency and queue limits.** Free GitHub Actions tier has concurrency limits that bite at scale (20 concurrent jobs free, 180 paid). Jenkins has no such limit but you size the agent fleet. GitLab CI has runner concurrency settings.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GitHub Actions is the default for GitHub-hosted teams** — zero setup, marketplace ecosystem, OIDC to clouds; great until you hit huge minute counts
- **Jenkins wins for self-hosted, regulated, or multi-cloud complexity** — 1,800+ plugins, full control; you pay in operational burden (LTS upgrades, plugin rot)
- **GitLab CI wins for tool consolidation** — repo + CI + registry + scanning + deploy in one product; best when you want fewer tools
- **Self-hosted runner security matters** — PR code on your runner is dangerous; use ephemeral runners and restrict fork PR triggering
- **OIDC over static credentials** — all three support cloud OIDC; eliminates secret rotation and stolen-credential risk
- **Vendor lock-in differs** — Jenkinsfiles are portable; GitHub composite actions and GitLab YAML lock you into the platform

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All three tools build, test, and deploy. The choice comes down to where your code lives, how much operational burden you can carry, and whether you want a focused tool or a consolidated platform.

**GitHub Actions — the default for GitHub-hosted teams**
- Pipelines live in `.github/workflows/`; runs on GitHub-hosted runners with a 2,000-minute monthly free tier on private repos and unlimited on public
- Marketplace has 20,000+ actions — Docker login, AWS credentials, Slack notifications all available as one-line includes
- Tight PR integration: checks, deployments, environments all show up in the PR UX; OIDC to AWS/Azure/GCP eliminates long-lived secrets
- Best when you're on GitHub and want minimum setup; gets expensive past about 50,000 minutes per month, where self-hosted runners become cheaper but reintroduce operational burden

**Jenkins — self-hosted, plugin-rich, ultimate control**
- The original CI server; you run the controller, manage agents, patch plugins, handle security
- 1,800+ plugins cover virtually every tool ever created — mainframe deploys, proprietary scanners, niche cloud APIs
- Wins for air-gapped environments, regulated workloads where code can't leave your perimeter, multi-cloud complexity that no SaaS tool integrates with, or teams with deep existing investment
- The cost is real — LTS upgrades break plugin combinations, security advisories pile up, you need a dedicated platform team for any serious Jenkins deployment

**GitLab CI — the consolidation play**
- Built into GitLab; pipelines in `.gitlab-ci.yml`; available as SaaS or self-hosted
- Killer feature is integration: container registry, package registry, SAST, DAST, dependency scanning, container scanning, license scanning, Kubernetes deploy all in one product
- Best when you want one tool for repo plus CI plus registry plus scanning plus deploy — fewer tools, fewer integrations to maintain
- The catch: lock-in to GitLab; if you outgrow it, migrating means rewriting pipelines and finding replacements for every built-in feature

**Hidden traps to call out**
- Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners run untrusted PR code; without isolation, a malicious PR exfiltrates your runner secrets; use ephemeral runners and restrict fork PRs
- Plugin rot in Jenkins is real — a 100-plugin instance is a security and stability liability; budget for ongoing maintenance or use a managed offering
- Vendor lock-in differs sharply: Jenkinsfiles are portable across hosts; composite actions and GitLab YAML are not

**The default recommendation**
- New team on GitHub: GitHub Actions, OIDC to cloud, self-hosted runners only when minute costs justify the operational burden
- Regulated or air-gapped: Jenkins with disciplined plugin hygiene, or GitLab self-hosted if you want better UX
- Tool consolidation goal: GitLab CI — one product, one source of truth

questions.question: Trunk-based development vs GitFlow vs GitHub flow — which branching model and when?
questions.title: Branching Models Compared: Trunk-Based, GitFlow, GitHub Flow
questions.direct_answer: Trunk-based wins for teams shipping multiple times a day with strong CI: short-lived branches (<1 day), feature flags for incomplete work, and main is always deployable — the model used by Google, Facebook, and most modern SaaS teams. GitFlow (develop, release, feature, hotfix branches) wins for software with explicit released versions — desktop apps, libraries, embedded firmware. GitHub flow (main + short-lived feature branches via PR) is the simple middle ground — great for small teams.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of CI/CD branching strategy and its impact on velocity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adopting GitFlow for a SaaS web app — the develop/release branches add overhead with no benefit when there are no released versions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss branch lifetime as the key metric, the relationship between trunk-based and feature flags, and the merge-conflict cost of long-lived branches

sections.title: Branching Strategy Determines Your CI/CD Velocity Ceiling
sections.content:
The branching model is not a stylistic choice — it sets the ceiling on how often you can deploy. A model with long-lived branches (release/develop) makes continuous deployment effectively impossible because every merge becomes a multi-branch coordination problem. A model with short-lived branches off main makes daily deploys natural.

**Trunk-based development** keeps a single long-lived branch (main/trunk) that is always deployable. Developers create short-lived branches (less than 1 day, ideally a few hours), open PRs, get review, and merge. Incomplete features hide behind feature flags. CI runs on every commit; if main breaks, the team stops to fix it. Used by Google, Facebook, Netflix, Stripe — any team shipping many times per day.

**GitFlow** (Vincent Driessen, 2010) introduces multiple long-lived branches: `master` (production), `develop` (next release), `feature/*` (new work, branch from develop), `release/*` (release stabilization), `hotfix/*` (production fixes). Optimized for software with explicit version releases — you cut a release branch, stabilize it, ship version 2.3.0, then keep developing on develop for 2.4.0. Hotfixes go to master and back-merge to develop.

**GitHub flow** is the simplification: main + short-lived feature branches via PR. No develop, no release branches. Merge to main = deployable. Used by GitHub itself and most small-to-medium SaaS teams; a stepping stone toward full trunk-based for teams not yet ready to ditch the PR-as-gating-step model.

sections.title: Three Branching Models Visualized
sections.content:
```mermaid
gitGraph
    commit id: "main"
    branch feature-a
    commit id: "work"
    commit id: "work2"
    checkout main
    merge feature-a id: "merge A"
    branch feature-b
    commit id: "work3"
    checkout main
    merge feature-b id: "merge B"
    commit id: "deploy"
```

**Trunk-based / GitHub flow**: short-lived branches off main, merge fast, deploy from main. The diagram shows the simple, fast pattern.

**GitFlow** (more complex): main + develop + feature/* + release/* + hotfix/*. Feature merges to develop; release branches cut from develop; release branches merge to both main (tagged) and develop. Hotfixes branch from main and merge back to both. The branch graph becomes a busy braid.

The simpler the graph, the faster you can deploy.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Trunk-Based | GitFlow | GitHub Flow |
|--------|-------------|---------|-------------|
| **Long-lived branches** | 1 (main) | 2 (master, develop) | 1 (main) |
| **Branch lifetime** | < 1 day, often hours | Weeks for features, months for releases | 1–3 days |
| **Deploy frequency ceiling** | Many per day | Per release cycle | Multiple per day |
| **Feature flags required?** | Yes — essential for incomplete work | Optional | Optional |
| **Merge conflict frequency** | Low (short branches) | High (long-lived develop) | Medium |
| **Best for** | SaaS, services, daily deploys | Released software with versions | Small–medium SaaS teams |
| **Examples** | Google, Facebook, Netflix, Stripe | Open-source libraries, desktop apps, firmware | GitHub, most early-stage startups |
| **CI requirement** | Strong (must catch breakage immediately) | Moderate | Strong |
| **Hotfix path** | PR to main + deploy | hotfix/* branch → master + back-merge | PR to main + deploy |
| **Learning curve** | Low (one branch) but discipline-heavy | High (multiple branch rules) | Lowest |
| **Code review model** | Small frequent PRs | Larger PRs at feature complete | Small frequent PRs |

sections.title: Decision Tree: Picking Your Model
sections.content:
**Pick trunk-based when:**
- You ship a SaaS service or web app with no explicit version concept
- You want or already do many deploys per day
- Your team has strong CI (fast tests, comprehensive coverage) and discipline to fix main when it breaks
- You're comfortable with feature flags as a first-class development tool
- Examples: any modern microservices platform, mature SaaS engineering org

**Pick GitFlow when:**
- You ship versioned releases that customers install (libraries, frameworks, desktop apps, mobile apps before continuous delivery)
- You need long stabilization periods on release branches
- You support multiple released versions in parallel (v2.x and v3.x both maintained)
- You have explicit release ceremonies, version numbers, and changelogs that matter to users
- Examples: open-source libraries, embedded firmware, regulated software with formal release sign-off

**Pick GitHub flow when:**
- You're a small–medium team on a SaaS product
- You want simpler than GitFlow but aren't ready for the discipline of trunk-based (no long-lived feature branches, feature flags everywhere)
- You value PR review as the primary quality gate
- You ship multiple times per week but not always multiple times per day
- Examples: most early-stage startups, GitHub itself

**The natural progression** for a growing team is GitHub flow → trunk-based as deploy frequency increases and feature-flag tooling matures. GitFlow is rarely the right answer for SaaS — it's a model designed for shipped software with versioned releases.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**Branch lifetime is the metric that matters.** A 2-week feature branch creates massive merge conflicts when finally merged — main has moved on, the diff is huge, and rebase/merge is painful. A 4-hour branch has minimal drift. The single biggest velocity unlock is shrinking branch lifetime; everything else (model name, PR template, review process) is secondary.

**Trunk-based requires feature flag discipline.** You can't merge half-built features without flags — they'd ship to production. Adopting trunk-based without a feature-flag system (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature, even simple environment variables) means you'll either avoid merging incomplete work (long branches return) or ship broken UX. Build the flag infrastructure first.

**GitFlow's `release/*` branches are an anti-pattern for SaaS.** A SaaS app has no "release" — you deploy continuously. Cutting a release branch, stabilizing it for a week, then merging back is friction with no benefit. Teams that adopt GitFlow for SaaS spend cycles fighting the model.

**The hotfix conundrum in GitFlow.** A production bug needs a hotfix. You branch from master, fix, merge to master, deploy. Now you must back-merge to develop — if you forget, the bug returns next release. This is the single most common GitFlow mistake.

**PRs vs commits in trunk-based.** Pure trunk-based at Google means committing directly to main with pre-commit review (Critique). Most companies use PRs as a lightweight gate while still calling it trunk-based — short-lived branch, fast review, merge same day. Both are valid; the key is short branch lifetime.

**Long-lived branches mask CI gaps.** If features sit on long branches, CI on main only catches breakage at merge time — too late. Trunk-based forces CI maturity because every commit is a deploy candidate.

**Squash vs merge commits.** Trunk-based teams typically squash-merge PRs to keep main history clean. GitFlow uses true merge commits to preserve branch topology. Style matters less than consistency.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Branch lifetime is the velocity metric** — short branches (<1 day) enable daily deploys; long branches make continuous deployment impossible
- **Trunk-based + feature flags** is the modern SaaS standard — used by Google, Facebook, Netflix, Stripe; enables many deploys per day
- **GitFlow is for versioned software** — libraries, desktop apps, firmware; SaaS adopting GitFlow fights the model
- **GitHub flow is the simpler middle ground** — main + short-lived feature branches via PR; common for small–medium teams
- **Feature flags are essential for trunk-based** — without them, incomplete work either ships broken or sits on long branches; build the flag infrastructure first
- **The natural progression**: GitHub flow → trunk-based as deploy frequency and feature-flag maturity grow

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Branching strategy isn't a stylistic choice — it sets the ceiling on how often you can deploy. The metric that matters is branch lifetime; everything else is secondary.

**Trunk-based development — the modern SaaS default**
- One long-lived branch (main); short-lived feature branches (less than a day, often hours); incomplete work hidden behind feature flags
- Used by Google, Facebook, Netflix, Stripe — any team that ships many times per day
- Requires strong CI (fast comprehensive tests) and discipline: when main breaks, the team stops to fix it before merging anything else
- Requires feature flags as a first-class tool — LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature, or in-house — because you can't merge half-built features without breaking production

**GitFlow — for versioned shipped software**
- Multiple long-lived branches: master (production), develop (next release), feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*
- Feature branches off develop, merge back; release branches cut from develop and stabilized then merged to master with a tag; hotfixes branch from master and back-merge to develop
- Optimized for software with explicit released versions — open-source libraries, desktop apps, embedded firmware, regulated software with formal release sign-off
- Anti-pattern for SaaS: a continuously-deployed service has no concept of a release, so the develop and release branches add overhead with no benefit

**GitHub flow — the simple middle ground**
- Main plus short-lived feature branches via PR; no develop, no release branches
- Used by GitHub itself and most small-to-medium SaaS teams; a stepping stone toward full trunk-based for teams not yet ready to ditch PR review as the gating step

**The metric that matters — branch lifetime**
- A 2-week feature branch creates massive merge conflicts when merged; a 4-hour branch has minimal drift
- The single biggest velocity unlock is shrinking branch lifetime; the model name (trunk-based vs GitHub flow) is secondary
- Long-lived branches mask CI gaps because main only sees breakage at merge time; trunk-based forces CI maturity

**Common mistakes**
- Adopting GitFlow for a SaaS web app — the develop and release branches solve a problem you don't have
- Adopting trunk-based without feature-flag tooling — incomplete work either ships broken or sits on long branches, defeating the purpose
- Forgetting to back-merge GitFlow hotfixes from master to develop — the bug returns in the next release
- Treating branch model as the goal rather than as a means to faster, safer deploys

**The default recommendation**
- New SaaS team: GitHub flow now, trunk-based as deploy frequency grows past once-per-day
- Library or desktop app with versioned releases: GitFlow makes sense
- Mature SaaS engineering org: trunk-based with feature flags, treating main as always-deployable
